node.name: Inverse functions
node.description: Reverse a one-to-one mapping and restrict the domain when needed.
node.details:
An inverse function undoes another function: if f sends 2 to 7, then f⁻¹ sends 7 back to 2. For f(x) = 2x + 3, solve y = 2x + 3 for x to get x = (y − 3)/2, then rename the variable: f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2. Checking that f(f⁻¹(x)) = x and f⁻¹(f(x)) = x confirms the result. The notation f⁻¹(x) means the inverse function, not 1/f(x).

Only one-to-one functions have inverses, because each output must trace back to a single input. A graph is one-to-one when no horizontal line meets it twice. f(x) = x² fails, since both 3 and −3 give 9, but restricting its domain to x ≥ 0 makes it one-to-one with inverse √x. The domain and range trade places between a function and its inverse, and the graph of f⁻¹ is the mirror image of f in the line y = x. Logarithms arise exactly this way, as inverses of exponential functions.

node.name: Inverse trigonometry and quadrants
node.description: Recover angles from ratios and resolve the quadrant ambiguity using both components.
node.details:
Inverse trigonometric functions run the trigonometric ratios backwards, turning a ratio into an angle. Because sine, cosine, and tangent repeat, each inverse returns only a principal value from a restricted range: arcsin gives angles from −90° to 90°, arccos from 0° to 180°, and arctan strictly between −90° and 90°. Other valid angles must be found using symmetry and the quadrant.

For example, arcsin(0.5) = 30°, but 150° also has sine 0.5. Direction problems show why quadrants matter. A vector with components x = −3 and y = −3 has tan θ = 1, and arctan(1) = 45°, yet the vector points into the third quadrant, so its direction is 225°. Using the signs of both components, as the two-argument function atan2(y, x) does in most programming languages, resolves this. Note that arcsin and arccos only accept inputs from −1 to 1. This skill is the gateway to solving trigonometric equations.

node.name: Work by a constant force
node.description: Calculate energy transfer through the component of force along displacement.
node.details:
A constant force does work W = F·d·cos θ on an object, where d is the displacement and θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. This is the same as the dot product F · d. The unit is the joule, 1 J = 1 N·m. Only the component of force along the motion counts. A 20 N pull at 60° above the direction of travel, over 3 m, does 20 × 3 × cos 60° = 30 J.

The sign of work tells you which way energy flows. Work is positive when the force has a component along the motion, and negative when it opposes the motion, as kinetic friction does on a sliding block. Work is zero when the force is perpendicular to the motion. For example, the normal force does no work on a cart rolling across level ground, and the inward force in circular motion changes direction without changing speed. Work is the bridge to kinetic and potential energy, and dividing it by time gives power.
